team.aggregation_rationale: mixed consensus (support=0.00, conditional=1.00, blockers=0) — non-blocking concerns warrant accelerated approval with PMRs.

major_deficiencies.description: Absence of a formal pre-specified null hypothesis and Type I error control for the primary ORR endpoint in CHRYSALIS. The application relies on a descriptive point estimate (ORR 40%, 95% CI: 29–51%) without a documented pre-specified alpha or hypothesis test. The lower bound of the CI (29%) approaches the upper bound of historical second-line chemotherapy ORR (~23% for ramucirumab+docetaxel), materially narrowing the demonstrated margin of clinical superiority and weakening the strength of statistical inference supporting the surrogate endpoint claim.

Immaturity and instability of Duration of Response (DOR) data: median DOR 11.1 months with upper 95% CI bound not estimable (NE), based on only 32 responders with 63% maintaining response ≥6 months at the October 2020 data cutoff. The Kaplan-Meier tail is unstable, no sensitivity analysis for informative censoring in the single-arm open-label setting is described, and the durability claim — a key component of the benefit-risk argument — rests on a small, heavily censored subset. This limits the reliability of DOR as a co-anchor of the accelerated approval surrogate endpoint package.

Absence of a validated tissue-based companion diagnostic (CDx) for EGFR exon 20 insertion detection at the time of BLA submission. Only the plasma-based Guardant360 CDx was reviewed contemporaneously. A tissue-based IVD is agreed as a post-marketing commitment (PMC) but is not yet fulfilled. Given that plasma-based liquid biopsy has known false-negative rates in NSCLC, the absence of a tissue CDx at approval creates a patient-selection quality gap that could result in both missed eligible patients and inappropriate use in non-harboring patients in the post-market real-world setting.

Dose optimization gap under Project Optimus principles: the body-weight-tiered RP2D (1050 mg for <80 kg; 1400 mg for ≥80 kg) was selected as the maximum tolerated/recommended Phase 2 dose from a Phase 1 dose-escalation study without a formal randomized dose-comparison arm or systematic exploration of lower doses or alternative schedules. The high rate of dose interruptions (78%) and dose reductions (15%) in CHRYSALIS indicates the RP2D may not be optimally positioned on the dose-toxicity curve. Exposure-response analyses show a positive ORR/PFS association across Ctrough tertiles without a clearly identified plateau, meaning a lower dose with a more favorable therapeutic index has not been ruled out. No dedicated dose-optimization study has been conducted or committed to.

Absence of dedicated renal and hepatic organ-impairment pharmacokinetic studies. Patients with moderate-to-severe renal or hepatic impairment are commonly encountered in the NSCLC population, yet no formal organ-impairment cohort data are available to validate or adjust dosing recommendations for these subgroups. The popPK model includes creatinine clearance as a covariate but does not substitute for a dedicated study, leaving prescribers without evidence-based dose guidance for a clinically important and vulnerable patient segment.

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients in the efficacy population (2.3% vs. ~9.4% in the Flatiron real-world EGFR exon 20ins NSCLC population), limiting generalizability of the ORR and safety estimates to the full U.S. target population. This demographic gap, consistently flagged across regulatory, clinical, and biostatistics disciplines, is not addressable through labeling alone and requires a prospective post-marketing commitment to enroll adequate numbers of underrepresented racial subgroups in the confirmatory PAPILLON trial or a dedicated post-marketing study.

Absence of a concentration-QTc analysis from clinical trial ECG data. No dedicated thorough QT study was conducted and no concentration-QTc analysis from CHRYSALIS ECG data is presented in the submission, which is expected per ICH E14/S7B guidance for oncology biologics. While large-molecule IgG1 biologics rarely cause direct QTc prolongation, the absence of this analysis leaves a characterizable cardiac safety gap unaddressed.

CMC comparability data adequacy across manufacturing scale-up (Phase I/II CHRYSALIS material vs. proposed commercial process) cannot be independently verified from the clinical summary. The bispecific IgG1 low-fucosylation format introduces complexity in aggregation, fragmentation, charge variant profiles, and arm-pairing fidelity that requires tight lot-to-lot control. Facility inspection classifications (VAI/NAI/OAI) for drug substance and drug product manufacturing sites are not explicitly confirmed in the available record.

blind_positions.summary: Amivantamab (RYBREVANT, BLA 761210) is a bispecific EGFR/MET antibody seeking accelerated approval for adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. The evidentiary package is anchored on a single-arm, open-label, multi-cohort Phase 1/2 trial (CHRYSALIS; Study 61186372EDI1001) in a precisely defined, biomarker-selected population of 81 patients. The confirmed ORR by BICR of 40% (95% CI: 29, 51) with a median DOR of 11.1 months (95% CI: 6.9, NE) is clinically meaningful against a backdrop of zero approved targeted therapies for this mutation subtype and a historical ORR of 10–23% with available second-line options. The indication as sought is tightly biomarker-restricted (EGFR exon 20 insertion, FDA-approved test, post-platinum), which is precisely the population studied; there is no mismatch between the label sought and the evidence generated. The accelerated approval pathway is appropriate given the surrogate endpoint (ORR/DOR), the unmet need, and the confirmatory Phase 3 trial (PAPILLON) already underway. Residual regulatory concerns — single-arm design limitations, underrepresentation of Black/African American patients, companion diagnostic tissue-based test PMC, and confirmatory trial PMR — are all addressable through labeling, post-marketing requirements, and commitments, and do not individually or collectively constitute a blocking deficiency. The benefit-risk balance supports conditional (accelerated) approval.
key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized trial design (CHRYSALIS) precludes direct causal attribution of ORR/DOR to amivantamab versus natural history or patient selection bias; no randomized OS or PFS data available at time of submission
Accelerated approval surrogate endpoint (ORR/DOR) requires verification of clinical benefit via confirmatory randomized trial (PAPILLON); PMR must be formally binding with agreed milestones
Efficacy population is small (N=81) with relatively limited follow-up; point estimate of ORR and DOR confidence intervals are wide, introducing uncertainty in the precision of the benefit estimate

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients (2.3% in efficacy population vs. ~9.4% in Flatiron real-world EGFR exon 20ins NSCLC population) limits generalizability; PMC agreed to but not yet fulfilled

Tissue-based companion diagnostic (CDx) for EGFR exon 20 insertion detection not yet approved at time of BLA submission; only plasma-based Guardant360 CDx reviewed contemporaneously; tissue CDx PMC must be enforced

Heterogeneity of EGFR exon 20 insertion subtypes (multiple distinct in-frame insertions) raises question of whether ORR is uniform across all subtypes; exploratory subgroup data by insertion subtype (FDA Table 11) show variability but sample sizes are too small for definitive conclusions
No direct comparative data against current second-line standard of care (docetaxel ± ramucirumab, anti-PD-(L)1) in this specific biomarker-defined population; cross-trial comparisons are confounded
Duration of follow-up at data cutoff (Oct 8, 2020) is limited; median OS not mature; long-term durability of responses and OS benefit remain unverified

blind_positions.summary: Amivantamab (RYBREVANT) is a bispecific EGFR/MET antibody evaluated in the CHRYSALIS trial (Study 61186372EDI1001), a single-arm, open-label, multi-cohort Phase 1/2 study. The primary efficacy population comprises 81 patients with metastatic NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations who had progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. BICR-assessed confirmed ORR was 40% (95% CI: 29, 51) with a median DOR of 11.1 months (95% CI: 6.9, NE), with 63% of responders maintaining response ≥6 months. This represents a clinically meaningful and durable response rate in a population with a well-characterized unmet medical need, where no targeted therapy was previously approved and second-line options yielded ORRs of only 10–23%. The safety profile — dominated by infusion-related reactions (~65%), rash, paronychia, and ILD/pneumonitis — is manageable through labeling, premedication, and dose modification guidance. On balance, the benefit-risk profile supports accelerated approval conditioned on post-marketing verification of clinical benefit via a randomized confirmatory trial.
key_concerns: Single-arm trial design precludes direct comparison of ORR or DOR to standard of care; no randomized OS or PFS data available at time of submission.
Primary efficacy population is small (N=81), limiting precision of ORR estimate (95% CI: 29–51%) and subgroup analyses.
Surrogate endpoint (ORR/DOR) used for accelerated approval — clinical benefit (OS, PFS) not yet verified in a randomized setting.
Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients (2.3% in efficacy population vs. ~9.4% in real-world Flatiron dataset), limiting generalizability.
Absence of a tissue-based companion diagnostic at time of approval; plasma-based CDx (Guardant360 CDx) approved contemporaneously but tissue-based IVD is a PMC.
Relatively limited follow-up duration at data cutoff (Oct 8, 2020); median DOR upper bound not estimable, introducing uncertainty about true durability.
High rate of dose interruptions (78% of patients), predominantly IRR-driven, raises tolerability concerns in a real-world setting outside clinical trial infrastructure.
ILD/pneumonitis, though low incidence (~4%), is potentially fatal and requires robust labeling guidance and monitoring recommendations.
No OS data mature enough to confirm survival benefit; median OS not reported as a primary or key secondary endpoint in the efficacy population at submission.
Confirmatory Phase 3 trial (amivantamab + carboplatin-pemetrexed vs. carboplatin-pemetrexed) ongoing but results not available — accelerated approval contingent on this verification.

deficiencies.description: Unverified surrogate endpoint as sole basis for approval: The application relies exclusively on ORR (40%) and DOR (median 11.1 months) from a single-arm, non-randomized trial (N=81) without mature OS or PFS data from a controlled study. While ORR is an accepted surrogate for accelerated approval in NSCLC per FDA guidance (Clinical Trial Endpoints for Approval of NSCLC Drugs and Biologics), the effect size and durability are promising but unconfirmed as predictors of OS benefit. This is not blocking given the accelerated approval pathway is appropriate here, but post-marketing verification via the ongoing Phase 3 randomized trial is required.

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients: Only 2.3% of the primary efficacy population identified as Black or African American, compared to ~9.4% in the real-world Flatiron Health dataset for this disease. This limits the ability to confirm that the observed benefit generalizes to this subgroup. Addressable via a post-marketing commitment (PMC) to submit clinical trial data characterizing safety and efficacy in this population, as agreed by the sponsor.

Absence of validated tissue-based companion diagnostic at time of approval: The contemporaneously approved CDx is plasma-based (Guardant360 CDx). A tissue-based IVD is not yet validated, which may limit patient identification in settings where liquid biopsy is not available or yields insufficient circulating tumor DNA. Addressable via the agreed PMC for tissue-based IVD analytical and clinical validation data.

blind_positions.summary: Amivantamab (JNJ-61186372) is a low-fucose, fully human IgG1 bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and MET. From a nonclinical safety perspective, the package is largely adequate for an accelerated approval in a life-threatening oncology indication under ICH S9 principles. The pivotal toxicology species (cynomolgus monkey) is pharmacologically relevant, with exposures at the high dose (~5x human AUC at RP2D) providing an adequate safety margin. Key nonclinical findings (GI mucosal erosion/hemorrhage, renal tubular regeneration, hepatic Kupffer cell changes) are consistent with the known biology of EGFR/MET inhibition and are reflected in clinical adverse events (rash, paronychia, ILD/pneumonitis, edema). The weight-of-evidence approach to embryofetal developmental toxicity is acceptable under ICH S9 for an advanced cancer indication, and the reproductive risk is adequately communicated in labeling. The principal nonclinical safety concern from a Project Optimus lens is that dose selection was driven by a body-weight-tiered RP2D without a formal dose-optimization study exploring lower doses or alternative schedules for a better therapeutic index; however, the clinical exposure-response data provided partially mitigate this gap. No single nonclinical finding rises to the level of a blocking deficiency warranting a Complete Response Letter.
key_concerns: Absence of a dedicated embryofetal development (EFD) study in a pharmacologically relevant species (cynomolgus monkey); weight-of-evidence approach accepted under ICH S9 but leaves residual uncertainty about teratogenic potential specific to amivantamab's dual EGFR/MET blockade.

Project Optimus dose-optimization gap: the RP2D (1050/1400 mg weight-tiered) was selected as the maximum tolerated/recommended Phase 2 dose from a Phase 1 dose-escalation study without a formal randomized dose-comparison arm or systematic exploration of lower doses/alternative schedules to establish a more favorable therapeutic index. The high rate of dose interruptions (78%) and dose reductions (15%) in the clinical trial suggests the RP2D may not be optimally positioned on the dose-toxicity curve.

GI mucosal erosion and hemorrhage observed in the 13-week cynomolgus monkey study at all dose levels (including 60 mg/kg, the lower dose group) are non-dose-dependent, raising questions about a threshold for this finding and its clinical correlate (nausea, vomiting, stomatitis seen in ≥20% of patients).

No dedicated safety pharmacology studies (cardiovascular, CNS, respiratory) were submitted as standalone GLP studies; reliance on integrated assessment within the repeat-dose toxicology study is acceptable under ICH S9 for a biologic but limits characterization of off-target safety pharmacology signals.
Renal tubular regeneration and mixed cell infiltration observed in monkeys at all dose levels — clinical correlate (edema, potential nephrotoxicity) warrants continued post-marketing monitoring.

Lack of rat or mouse pharmacological activity (amivantamab does not bind rat EGFR or MET) limits the ability to conduct standard rodent reproductive/developmental toxicology; the weight-of-evidence package relies heavily on surrogate molecules (lazertinib in rats, zalutumumab in monkeys), which may not fully capture the dual EGFR+MET blockade pharmacology of amivantamab.
No carcinogenicity studies — acceptable under ICH S9 for advanced cancer indication but should be noted.

Subcutaneous formulation TK data (JNJ-61186372 with rHuPH20) included in the package is for a route not proposed in this BLA; its relevance to the IV formulation safety assessment is limited and could create labeling confusion.

deficiencies.description: Project Optimus dose-optimization deficiency: The RP2D (1050 mg for <80 kg; 1400 mg for ≥80 kg IV) was selected based on traditional Phase 1 MTD/RP2D paradigm without a randomized dose-comparison or systematic lower-dose exploration. The clinical safety database shows 78% of patients required dose interruptions and 15% required dose reductions, predominantly driven by IRR, rash, and paronychia — suggesting the RP2D sits at or near the top of the tolerability curve. Under Project Optimus expectations, the sponsor has not demonstrated that this dose represents an optimized therapeutic index rather than simply the highest tolerated dose. This is a reviewable deficiency addressable via a post-marketing requirement (PMR) for a randomized dose-optimization study, not a blocking issue for accelerated approval in a life-threatening indication with unmet need.

Incomplete embryofetal developmental toxicity characterization: No dedicated GLP EFD study was conducted with amivantamab in a pharmacologically relevant species. The weight-of-evidence package uses surrogate molecules (lazertinib [small molecule EGFR inhibitor] in rats; zalutumumab [anti-EGFR mAb, single target] in monkeys) that do not replicate the simultaneous dual EGFR+MET blockade of amivantamab. Given that MET deletion is embryonic lethal in mice and EGFR knockout causes severe developmental defects, the combined inhibition by amivantamab may carry additive or synergistic embryofetal risk not captured by either surrogate alone. This is addressable by labeling (strong embryofetal toxicity warning, contraception requirements) and is acceptable under ICH S9 for an advanced cancer indication; it does not warrant a CRL.

blind_positions.summary: Amivantamab (BLA 761210) presents a generally adequate clinical pharmacology package for accelerated approval in the targeted EGFR exon 20 insertion NSCLC population. The body-weight-based two-tier dosing strategy (1050 mg for <80 kg; 1400 mg for ≥80 kg) is supported by population PK modeling and exposure-response analyses demonstrating positive associations between higher trough concentrations (Ctrough.max, Ctrough.1st) and ORR, CBR, PFS, and OS, without a clearly identified plateau that would mandate dose de-escalation. Infusion-related reactions show a positive exposure-response relationship with end-of-infusion Cmax (Ceoi.1st), which is mechanistically plausible and supports the split-dose Week 1 administration strategy. Several clinical pharmacology gaps remain — most notably the absence of formal organ-impairment PK studies and limited DDI characterization — but these are addressable through labeling and post-marketing requirements given the biologic nature of the molecule and the serious/life-threatening indication. On balance, the clinical pharmacology data are sufficient to support conditional (accelerated) approval with post-marketing commitments.
key_concerns: Absence of dedicated renal and hepatic impairment PK studies: the popPK model includes creatinine clearance as a covariate for renal function, but no formal organ-impairment cohort data are available to validate dose recommendations in patients with moderate-to-severe renal or hepatic impairment, who are commonly encountered in the NSCLC population.

Dose optimization (Project Optimus lens): the exposure-response analyses show a positive ORR/PFS relationship across Ctrough tertiles without a clear plateau, raising the question of whether the lower dose tier (1050 mg) is fully optimized or whether a lower dose could retain efficacy with reduced IRR burden. However, the E-R safety analyses also show IRR is driven by Ceoi on Day 1 (first infusion), not steady-state AUC, limiting the actionability of dose reduction for the dominant toxicity.

Limited DDI characterization: amivantamab is a large-molecule IgG1 bispecific antibody and is not expected to be a CYP substrate or inhibitor; however, no formal assessment of the impact of concomitant small-molecule oncology agents (e.g., platinum agents, pemetrexed, or investigational lazertinib in the combination arm) on amivantamab PK or vice versa is presented in this monotherapy BLA. This is particularly relevant given the planned combination regimen.

Bioanalytical method validation: the popPK dataset relies on a single validated bioanalytical method; anti-drug antibody (ADA) prevalence and its impact on PK/exposure are not fully characterized in the submission, creating uncertainty about the exposure estimates in ADA-positive patients.

Subcutaneous formulation PK (JNJ-61186372 + rHuPH20): TK data from the SC route are presented in the monkey toxicology section (Table 10), suggesting a SC formulation is under development. No clinical PK bridging data are available; this is not a concern for the current IV BLA but should be flagged for future submissions.

Exposure-response for the ≥80 kg subgroup (1400 mg dose tier): the forest plot of ORR by subgroup and the popPK simulations (Figure 30) support similar steady-state exposures across weight tiers, but the number of patients in the ≥80 kg group is small, limiting precision of the E-R characterization in this subgroup.

QTc assessment: no dedicated thorough QT study was conducted. While large-molecule biologics rarely cause direct QTc prolongation, the submission does not include a concentration-QTc analysis from the clinical trial ECG data, which is expected per ICH E14/S7B guidance for oncology biologics.

deficiencies.description: Absence of formal renal and hepatic impairment PK studies: No dedicated organ-impairment cohorts were enrolled. The popPK model incorporates creatinine clearance as a covariate and shows modest effects on clearance, but the model has not been externally validated in patients with moderate-to-severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) or hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B/C). Labeling currently cannot provide evidence-based dose guidance for these subgroups, who represent a clinically meaningful fraction of the NSCLC population. This is addressable through a post-marketing requirement (PMR) to conduct organ-impairment PK studies, with interim labeling language acknowledging the limitation. It does not rise to the level of a Complete Response Letter for this life-threatening indication with unmet need.

Incomplete exposure-response characterization for the combination regimen context: The E-R analyses presented are derived exclusively from the amivantamab monotherapy cohort of CHRYSALIS. The ongoing Phase 3 confirmatory study evaluates amivantamab in combination with carboplatin-pemetrexed. No PK interaction data or E-R modeling for the combination are available in this BLA. While this is expected at the time of accelerated approval, a PMR to characterize combination PK and E-R is warranted. This is not blocking for the monotherapy indication as sought.

Absence of concentration-QTc analysis: No thorough QT study and no concentration-QTc analysis from on-study ECG data are presented. For a biologic of this class the risk is low, but the omission is a gap relative to current expectations. Addressable via a post-marketing commitment or labeling statement acknowledging the absence of dedicated QT data.

blind_positions.summary: From a biostatistics perspective, this accelerated approval application for amivantamab (RYBREVANT) in EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation NSCLC post-platinum chemotherapy is supported by a single-arm, open-label, multi-cohort trial (CHRYSALIS; Study 61186372EDI1001). The primary endpoint is overall response rate (ORR) assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR), with a confirmed ORR of 40% (95% CI: 29%, 51%) and median duration of response (DOR) of 11.1 months (95% CI: 6.9, NE) in 81 efficacy-evaluable patients. While the single-arm design and ORR endpoint are appropriate for accelerated approval in this rare, unmet-need oncology setting, several statistical concerns are identified — most notably the small, non-randomized efficacy population, the absence of a formal pre-specified hypothesis test with a controlled Type I error rate, and the immaturity of DOR data. These concerns are reviewable within the accelerated approval framework and are addressable via post-marketing requirements (confirmatory randomized trial already underway). No single statistical deficiency rises to the level of a blocking Complete Response Letter issue given the regulatory pathway chosen and the magnitude and durability of the observed effect. The statistical evidence is adequate to support conditional (accelerated) approval.
key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized design (CHRYSALIS) precludes causal inference; no concurrent control arm to benchmark ORR against standard of care, making attribution of response to amivantamab reliant on historical comparisons with inherent selection bias.

Small efficacy population (N=81): the 95% CI on ORR (29%, 51%) spans 22 percentage points, reflecting substantial imprecision. A true ORR as low as 29% cannot be excluded, which approaches the upper bound of historical chemotherapy ORR (~23% for ramucirumab+docetaxel) and reduces the margin of clinical superiority.

No formal pre-specified null hypothesis or Type I error control documented in the review materials. The application appears to rely on a descriptive point estimate rather than a hypothesis test with a pre-specified alpha, which is atypical even for single-arm accelerated approval submissions and limits the strength of the statistical inference.

Duration of Response (DOR) data are immature: median DOR 11.1 months with upper 95% CI bound 'not estimable' (NE), and only 63% of 32 responders had observed DOR ≥6 months at the October 2020 data cutoff. The durability claim rests on a small subset (n=32 responders) with censored observations, and the Kaplan-Meier estimate is unstable at the tail.

Multiplicity not formally controlled across secondary/exploratory endpoints (PFS, OS, CBR, PRO). Exposure-response analyses (ORR vs. Ctrough, PFS/OS by tertile) are exploratory and post-hoc in nature; any favorable signals from these analyses should not be used to strengthen the primary efficacy claim without pre-specification and multiplicity adjustment.

Potential for informative censoring in DOR and PFS analyses in a single-arm open-label trial: patients who discontinue due to toxicity or clinical deterioration may be censored in ways that inflate apparent response duration. No sensitivity analysis for informative censoring is described in the review materials.

Efficacy population definition (patients with first dose on or before 05 Feb 2020 at RP2D with exon 20 insertion and prior chemotherapy) involves post-hoc selection from a larger multi-cohort study, introducing potential for selection bias in the analysis set. The relationship between the pre-specified analysis population and the final efficacy population requires scrutiny.

Subgroup analyses (ORR by exon 20 insertion subtype, demographic subgroups) are exploratory and underpowered; the forest plot shows wide CIs across subgroups. These analyses are hypothesis-generating only and should not be used to restrict or expand the label without confirmatory data.

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients (2.3% in efficacy population vs. ~9.4% in Flatiron real-world data) limits generalizability of the statistical estimates to the full U.S. target population.

The 120-day update adds additional patients and follow-up, but the statistical framework for integrating updated data with the primary analysis (including any impact on the primary ORR estimate and CI) is not fully described, raising questions about whether the primary analysis was locked prior to unblinding.

blind_positions.summary: Amivantamab-vmjw (RYBREVANT, BLA 761210) is a low-fucose, fully human IgG1-based bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and MET. From a CMC perspective, the case package provided is a clinical multi-discipline review summary and does not contain the full OPQ (Office of Pharmaceutical Quality) technical review dossier. The available record references a Product Quality Review (April 23, 2021), a Quality Executive Summary (April 28, 2021), and a Quality Executive Summary Addendum (May 20, 2021), as well as Drug Substance and Drug Product Microbiology/Facility Reviews, all of which were completed prior to the May 20, 2021 review completion date. The cross-discipline summary indicates no blocking CMC deficiencies were identified by the OPQ reviewer (Andrea Franco) and that facility inspections, comparability strategy, shelf-life, and cell bank qualification were addressed through pre-submission meetings. A post-marketing commitment (PMC) was agreed upon for the tissue-based companion diagnostic IVD, which is a device/CDx matter rather than a drug CMC issue. The low-fucosylation engineering (relevant to ADCC potency and lot-to-lot consistency) and the bispecific format (relevant to aggregation, fragmentation, and charge variant control) are inherent complexity factors for this molecule, but the available record does not surface any unresolved deficiencies in these areas. The formulation (350 mg/7 mL, 50 mg/mL single-dose vial) is straightforward for a monoclonal antibody-class biologic. On the basis of the available record, CMC does not independently block approval, though the complexity of the molecule warrants ongoing post-market stability and comparability vigilance.
key_concerns: Limited CMC detail visible in this case package: the full OPQ technical review (impurity characterization, control strategy, process validation data, extended stability data) is not reproduced here, creating residual uncertainty in this assessment.

Bispecific IgG1 format with low-fucosylation engineering introduces complexity: aggregation, fragmentation, charge variant profiles, and DAR-analog consistency (arm-pairing fidelity) must be tightly controlled and are not directly assessable from the clinical summary alone.

Stability data adequacy (ICH Q1): the pre-submission meetings confirmed a shelf-life strategy and a 30-day post-submission stability update was agreed upon, but the actual stability data package and confirmed shelf-life claim are not visible in this review document.

Comparability across manufacturing scale-up (Phase I/II material used in CHRYSALIS vs. proposed commercial process): pre-submission meetings addressed this, but the adequacy of the comparability exercise (PK bridging, functional assays, physicochemical characterization) cannot be independently verified from the clinical summary.

Cell bank qualification: a Type B CMC meeting confirmed the qualification strategy for future working cell banks, but the completion status of this qualification at the time of BLA submission is not confirmed in the available record.

Facility inspection status: the Quality Executive Summary and Addendum are referenced but not reproduced; no inspection classification (VAI/NAI/OAI) for the drug substance or drug product manufacturing facilities is explicitly stated in the clinical summary.

Post-marketing commitment for tissue-based companion diagnostic IVD (EGFR exon 20 insertion detection): while primarily a CDRH/CDx matter, the absence of a validated tissue-based test at approval has indirect implications for patient selection quality in the post-market setting.

deficiencies.description: Incomplete CMC data visibility in the case package: The full OPQ technical review covering impurity characterization and control strategy (ICH Q3/Q6B), extended real-time stability data supporting the proposed shelf-life claim (ICH Q1), and process validation data for the commercial-scale bispecific manufacturing process are not reproduced in the available multi-discipline review summary. For a low-fucose bispecific IgG1, these are critical quality attributes. However, the referenced OPQ reviews (April–May 2021) appear to have been completed, and pre-submission meetings resolved key strategic questions. This is assessed as a documentation/visibility gap in the case package rather than a confirmed unresolved deficiency, and is therefore treated as non-blocking pending confirmation that the OPQ review reached an approvable conclusion.

Comparability of CHRYSALIS clinical material to proposed commercial process: Amivantamab used in the pivotal CHRYSALIS study must be demonstrated comparable to the commercial-scale drug product via a robust physicochemical, functional (ADCC, receptor binding, bispecific arm-pairing), and PK bridging package. Pre-submission meetings indicate FDA accepted the comparability strategy, but the adequacy of the executed comparability data cannot be independently confirmed from the clinical summary. If the OPQ review identified residual gaps, this could be approval-limiting. Assessed as non-blocking given the pre-submission alignment, but flagged for confirmation.

Shelf-life and cold-chain stability for a bispecific antibody: The 350 mg/7 mL single-dose vial formulation must have adequate real-time and accelerated stability data (ICH Q1A(R2)) demonstrating control of aggregation, fragmentation, and potency loss over the proposed shelf-life. A 30-day post-submission stability update was agreed upon pre-BLA. The completion and adequacy of this update is not confirmed in the available record. Assessed as non-blocking given the agreed update mechanism, but requires OPQ confirmation.

Efficacy population is small (N=81) with relatively limited follow-up; point estimate of ORR and DOR confidence intervals are wide, introducing uncertainty in the precision of the benefit estimate

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients (2.3% in efficacy population vs. ~9.4% in Flatiron real-world EGFR exon 20ins NSCLC population) limits generalizability; PMC agreed to but not yet fulfilled

Tissue-based companion diagnostic (CDx) for EGFR exon 20 insertion detection not yet approved at time of BLA submission; only plasma-based Guardant360 CDx reviewed contemporaneously; tissue CDx PMC must be enforced

Heterogeneity of EGFR exon 20 insertion subtypes (multiple distinct in-frame insertions) raises question of whether ORR is uniform across all subtypes; exploratory subgroup data by insertion subtype (FDA Table 11) show variability but sample sizes are too small for definitive conclusions
No direct comparative data against current second-line standard of care (docetaxel ± ramucirumab, anti-PD-(L)1) in this specific biomarker-defined population; cross-trial comparisons are confounded
Duration of follow-up at data cutoff (Oct 8, 2020) is limited; median OS not mature; long-term durability of responses and OS benefit remain unverified

final_positions.summary: Amivantamab (RYBREVANT) is a bispecific EGFR/MET antibody evaluated in the CHRYSALIS trial (Study 61186372EDI1001), a single-arm, open-label, multi-cohort Phase 1/2 study. The primary efficacy population comprises 81 patients with metastatic NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations who had progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. BICR-assessed confirmed ORR was 40% (95% CI: 29, 51) with a median DOR of 11.1 months (95% CI: 6.9, NE), with 63% of responders maintaining response ≥6 months. This represents a clinically meaningful and durable response rate in a population with a well-characterized unmet medical need, where no targeted therapy was previously approved and second-line options yielded ORRs of only 10–23%. The safety profile — dominated by infusion-related reactions (~65%), rash, paronychia, and ILD/pneumonitis — is manageable through labeling, premedication, and dose modification guidance. On balance, the benefit-risk profile supports accelerated approval conditioned on post-marketing verification of clinical benefit via a randomized confirmatory trial.
key_concerns: Single-arm trial design precludes direct comparison of ORR or DOR to standard of care; no randomized OS or PFS data available at time of submission.
Primary efficacy population is small (N=81), limiting precision of ORR estimate (95% CI: 29–51%) and subgroup analyses.
Surrogate endpoint (ORR/DOR) used for accelerated approval — clinical benefit (OS, PFS) not yet verified in a randomized setting.
Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients (2.3% in efficacy population vs. ~9.4% in real-world Flatiron dataset), limiting generalizability.
Absence of a tissue-based companion diagnostic at time of approval; plasma-based CDx (Guardant360 CDx) approved contemporaneously but tissue-based IVD is a PMC.
Relatively limited follow-up duration at data cutoff (Oct 8, 2020); median DOR upper bound not estimable, introducing uncertainty about true durability.
High rate of dose interruptions (78% of patients), predominantly IRR-driven, raises tolerability concerns in a real-world setting outside clinical trial infrastructure.
ILD/pneumonitis, though low incidence (~4%), is potentially fatal and requires robust labeling guidance and monitoring recommendations.
No OS data mature enough to confirm survival benefit; median OS not reported as a primary or key secondary endpoint in the efficacy population at submission.
Confirmatory Phase 3 trial (amivantamab + carboplatin-pemetrexed vs. carboplatin-pemetrexed) ongoing but results not available — accelerated approval contingent on this verification.

deficiencies.description: Unverified surrogate endpoint as sole basis for approval: The application relies exclusively on ORR (40%) and DOR (median 11.1 months) from a single-arm, non-randomized trial (N=81) without mature OS or PFS data from a controlled study. While ORR is an accepted surrogate for accelerated approval in NSCLC per FDA guidance (Clinical Trial Endpoints for Approval of NSCLC Drugs and Biologics), the effect size and durability are promising but unconfirmed as predictors of OS benefit. This is not blocking given the accelerated approval pathway is appropriate here, but post-marketing verification via the ongoing Phase 3 randomized trial is required.

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients: Only 2.3% of the primary efficacy population identified as Black or African American, compared to ~9.4% in the real-world Flatiron Health dataset for this disease. This limits the ability to confirm that the observed benefit generalizes to this subgroup. Addressable via a post-marketing commitment (PMC) to submit clinical trial data characterizing safety and efficacy in this population, as agreed by the sponsor.

Absence of validated tissue-based companion diagnostic at time of approval: The contemporaneously approved CDx is plasma-based (Guardant360 CDx). A tissue-based IVD is not yet validated, which may limit patient identification in settings where liquid biopsy is not available or yields insufficient circulating tumor DNA. Addressable via the agreed PMC for tissue-based IVD analytical and clinical validation data.

final_positions.summary: Amivantamab (JNJ-61186372) is a low-fucose, fully human IgG1 bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and MET. From a nonclinical safety perspective, the package is largely adequate for an accelerated approval in a life-threatening oncology indication under ICH S9 principles. The pivotal toxicology species (cynomolgus monkey) is pharmacologically relevant, with exposures at the high dose (~5x human AUC at RP2D) providing an adequate safety margin. Key nonclinical findings (GI mucosal erosion/hemorrhage, renal tubular regeneration, hepatic Kupffer cell changes) are consistent with the known biology of EGFR/MET inhibition and are reflected in clinical adverse events (rash, paronychia, ILD/pneumonitis, edema). The weight-of-evidence approach to embryofetal developmental toxicity is acceptable under ICH S9 for an advanced cancer indication, and the reproductive risk is adequately communicated in labeling. The principal nonclinical safety concern from a Project Optimus lens is that dose selection was driven by a body-weight-tiered RP2D without a formal dose-optimization study exploring lower doses or alternative schedules for a better therapeutic index; however, the clinical exposure-response data provided partially mitigate this gap. No single nonclinical finding rises to the level of a blocking deficiency warranting a Complete Response Letter.
key_concerns: Absence of a dedicated embryofetal development (EFD) study in a pharmacologically relevant species (cynomolgus monkey); weight-of-evidence approach accepted under ICH S9 but leaves residual uncertainty about teratogenic potential specific to amivantamab's dual EGFR/MET blockade.

Project Optimus dose-optimization gap: the RP2D (1050/1400 mg weight-tiered) was selected as the maximum tolerated/recommended Phase 2 dose from a Phase 1 dose-escalation study without a formal randomized dose-comparison arm or systematic exploration of lower doses/alternative schedules to establish a more favorable therapeutic index. The high rate of dose interruptions (78%) and dose reductions (15%) in the clinical trial suggests the RP2D may not be optimally positioned on the dose-toxicity curve.

GI mucosal erosion and hemorrhage observed in the 13-week cynomolgus monkey study at all dose levels (including 60 mg/kg, the lower dose group) are non-dose-dependent, raising questions about a threshold for this finding and its clinical correlate (nausea, vomiting, stomatitis seen in ≥20% of patients).

No dedicated safety pharmacology studies (cardiovascular, CNS, respiratory) were submitted as standalone GLP studies; reliance on integrated assessment within the repeat-dose toxicology study is acceptable under ICH S9 for a biologic but limits characterization of off-target safety pharmacology signals.
Renal tubular regeneration and mixed cell infiltration observed in monkeys at all dose levels — clinical correlate (edema, potential nephrotoxicity) warrants continued post-marketing monitoring.

Lack of rat or mouse pharmacological activity (amivantamab does not bind rat EGFR or MET) limits the ability to conduct standard rodent reproductive/developmental toxicology; the weight-of-evidence package relies heavily on surrogate molecules (lazertinib in rats, zalutumumab in monkeys), which may not fully capture the dual EGFR+MET blockade pharmacology of amivantamab.
No carcinogenicity studies — acceptable under ICH S9 for advanced cancer indication but should be noted.

Subcutaneous formulation TK data (JNJ-61186372 with rHuPH20) included in the package is for a route not proposed in this BLA; its relevance to the IV formulation safety assessment is limited and could create labeling confusion.

deficiencies.description: Project Optimus dose-optimization deficiency: The RP2D (1050 mg for <80 kg; 1400 mg for ≥80 kg IV) was selected based on traditional Phase 1 MTD/RP2D paradigm without a randomized dose-comparison or systematic lower-dose exploration. The clinical safety database shows 78% of patients required dose interruptions and 15% required dose reductions, predominantly driven by IRR, rash, and paronychia — suggesting the RP2D sits at or near the top of the tolerability curve. Under Project Optimus expectations, the sponsor has not demonstrated that this dose represents an optimized therapeutic index rather than simply the highest tolerated dose. This is a reviewable deficiency addressable via a post-marketing requirement (PMR) for a randomized dose-optimization study, not a blocking issue for accelerated approval in a life-threatening indication with unmet need.

Incomplete embryofetal developmental toxicity characterization: No dedicated GLP EFD study was conducted with amivantamab in a pharmacologically relevant species. The weight-of-evidence package uses surrogate molecules (lazertinib [small molecule EGFR inhibitor] in rats; zalutumumab [anti-EGFR mAb, single target] in monkeys) that do not replicate the simultaneous dual EGFR+MET blockade of amivantamab. Given that MET deletion is embryonic lethal in mice and EGFR knockout causes severe developmental defects, the combined inhibition by amivantamab may carry additive or synergistic embryofetal risk not captured by either surrogate alone. This is addressable by labeling (strong embryofetal toxicity warning, contraception requirements) and is acceptable under ICH S9 for an advanced cancer indication; it does not warrant a CRL.

final_positions.summary: Amivantamab (BLA 761210) presents a generally adequate clinical pharmacology package for accelerated approval in the targeted EGFR exon 20 insertion NSCLC population. The body-weight-based two-tier dosing strategy (1050 mg for <80 kg; 1400 mg for ≥80 kg) is supported by population PK modeling and exposure-response analyses demonstrating positive associations between higher trough concentrations (Ctrough.max, Ctrough.1st) and ORR, CBR, PFS, and OS, without a clearly identified plateau that would mandate dose de-escalation. Infusion-related reactions show a positive exposure-response relationship with end-of-infusion Cmax (Ceoi.1st), which is mechanistically plausible and supports the split-dose Week 1 administration strategy. Several clinical pharmacology gaps remain — most notably the absence of formal organ-impairment PK studies and limited DDI characterization — but these are addressable through labeling and post-marketing requirements given the biologic nature of the molecule and the serious/life-threatening indication. On balance, the clinical pharmacology data are sufficient to support conditional (accelerated) approval with post-marketing commitments.
key_concerns: Absence of dedicated renal and hepatic impairment PK studies: the popPK model includes creatinine clearance as a covariate for renal function, but no formal organ-impairment cohort data are available to validate dose recommendations in patients with moderate-to-severe renal or hepatic impairment, who are commonly encountered in the NSCLC population.

Dose optimization (Project Optimus lens): the exposure-response analyses show a positive ORR/PFS relationship across Ctrough tertiles without a clear plateau, raising the question of whether the lower dose tier (1050 mg) is fully optimized or whether a lower dose could retain efficacy with reduced IRR burden. However, the E-R safety analyses also show IRR is driven by Ceoi on Day 1 (first infusion), not steady-state AUC, limiting the actionability of dose reduction for the dominant toxicity.

Limited DDI characterization: amivantamab is a large-molecule IgG1 bispecific antibody and is not expected to be a CYP substrate or inhibitor; however, no formal assessment of the impact of concomitant small-molecule oncology agents (e.g., platinum agents, pemetrexed, or investigational lazertinib in the combination arm) on amivantamab PK or vice versa is presented in this monotherapy BLA. This is particularly relevant given the planned combination regimen.

Bioanalytical method validation: the popPK dataset relies on a single validated bioanalytical method; anti-drug antibody (ADA) prevalence and its impact on PK/exposure are not fully characterized in the submission, creating uncertainty about the exposure estimates in ADA-positive patients.

Subcutaneous formulation PK (JNJ-61186372 + rHuPH20): TK data from the SC route are presented in the monkey toxicology section (Table 10), suggesting a SC formulation is under development. No clinical PK bridging data are available; this is not a concern for the current IV BLA but should be flagged for future submissions.

Exposure-response for the ≥80 kg subgroup (1400 mg dose tier): the forest plot of ORR by subgroup and the popPK simulations (Figure 30) support similar steady-state exposures across weight tiers, but the number of patients in the ≥80 kg group is small, limiting precision of the E-R characterization in this subgroup.

QTc assessment: no dedicated thorough QT study was conducted. While large-molecule biologics rarely cause direct QTc prolongation, the submission does not include a concentration-QTc analysis from the clinical trial ECG data, which is expected per ICH E14/S7B guidance for oncology biologics.

deficiencies.description: Absence of formal renal and hepatic impairment PK studies: No dedicated organ-impairment cohorts were enrolled. The popPK model incorporates creatinine clearance as a covariate and shows modest effects on clearance, but the model has not been externally validated in patients with moderate-to-severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) or hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B/C). Labeling currently cannot provide evidence-based dose guidance for these subgroups, who represent a clinically meaningful fraction of the NSCLC population. This is addressable through a post-marketing requirement (PMR) to conduct organ-impairment PK studies, with interim labeling language acknowledging the limitation. It does not rise to the level of a Complete Response Letter for this life-threatening indication with unmet need.

Incomplete exposure-response characterization for the combination regimen context: The E-R analyses presented are derived exclusively from the amivantamab monotherapy cohort of CHRYSALIS. The ongoing Phase 3 confirmatory study evaluates amivantamab in combination with carboplatin-pemetrexed. No PK interaction data or E-R modeling for the combination are available in this BLA. While this is expected at the time of accelerated approval, a PMR to characterize combination PK and E-R is warranted. This is not blocking for the monotherapy indication as sought.

Absence of concentration-QTc analysis: No thorough QT study and no concentration-QTc analysis from on-study ECG data are presented. For a biologic of this class the risk is low, but the omission is a gap relative to current expectations. Addressable via a post-marketing commitment or labeling statement acknowledging the absence of dedicated QT data.

final_positions.summary: From a biostatistics perspective, this accelerated approval application for amivantamab (RYBREVANT) in EGFR exon 20 insertion mutation NSCLC post-platinum chemotherapy is supported by a single-arm, open-label, multi-cohort trial (CHRYSALIS; Study 61186372EDI1001). The primary endpoint is overall response rate (ORR) assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR), with a confirmed ORR of 40% (95% CI: 29%, 51%) and median duration of response (DOR) of 11.1 months (95% CI: 6.9, NE) in 81 efficacy-evaluable patients. While the single-arm design and ORR endpoint are appropriate for accelerated approval in this rare, unmet-need oncology setting, several statistical concerns are identified — most notably the small, non-randomized efficacy population, the absence of a formal pre-specified hypothesis test with a controlled Type I error rate, and the immaturity of DOR data. These concerns are reviewable within the accelerated approval framework and are addressable via post-marketing requirements (confirmatory randomized trial already underway). No single statistical deficiency rises to the level of a blocking Complete Response Letter issue given the regulatory pathway chosen and the magnitude and durability of the observed effect. The statistical evidence is adequate to support conditional (accelerated) approval.
key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized design (CHRYSALIS) precludes causal inference; no concurrent control arm to benchmark ORR against standard of care, making attribution of response to amivantamab reliant on historical comparisons with inherent selection bias.

Small efficacy population (N=81): the 95% CI on ORR (29%, 51%) spans 22 percentage points, reflecting substantial imprecision. A true ORR as low as 29% cannot be excluded, which approaches the upper bound of historical chemotherapy ORR (~23% for ramucirumab+docetaxel) and reduces the margin of clinical superiority.

No formal pre-specified null hypothesis or Type I error control documented in the review materials. The application appears to rely on a descriptive point estimate rather than a hypothesis test with a pre-specified alpha, which is atypical even for single-arm accelerated approval submissions and limits the strength of the statistical inference.

Duration of Response (DOR) data are immature: median DOR 11.1 months with upper 95% CI bound 'not estimable' (NE), and only 63% of 32 responders had observed DOR ≥6 months at the October 2020 data cutoff. The durability claim rests on a small subset (n=32 responders) with censored observations, and the Kaplan-Meier estimate is unstable at the tail.

Multiplicity not formally controlled across secondary/exploratory endpoints (PFS, OS, CBR, PRO). Exposure-response analyses (ORR vs. Ctrough, PFS/OS by tertile) are exploratory and post-hoc in nature; any favorable signals from these analyses should not be used to strengthen the primary efficacy claim without pre-specification and multiplicity adjustment.

Potential for informative censoring in DOR and PFS analyses in a single-arm open-label trial: patients who discontinue due to toxicity or clinical deterioration may be censored in ways that inflate apparent response duration. No sensitivity analysis for informative censoring is described in the review materials.

Efficacy population definition (patients with first dose on or before 05 Feb 2020 at RP2D with exon 20 insertion and prior chemotherapy) involves post-hoc selection from a larger multi-cohort study, introducing potential for selection bias in the analysis set. The relationship between the pre-specified analysis population and the final efficacy population requires scrutiny.

Subgroup analyses (ORR by exon 20 insertion subtype, demographic subgroups) are exploratory and underpowered; the forest plot shows wide CIs across subgroups. These analyses are hypothesis-generating only and should not be used to restrict or expand the label without confirmatory data.

Underrepresentation of Black/African American patients (2.3% in efficacy population vs. ~9.4% in Flatiron real-world data) limits generalizability of the statistical estimates to the full U.S. target population.

The 120-day update adds additional patients and follow-up, but the statistical framework for integrating updated data with the primary analysis (including any impact on the primary ORR estimate and CI) is not fully described, raising questions about whether the primary analysis was locked prior to unblinding.

final_positions.summary: Amivantamab-vmjw (RYBREVANT, BLA 761210) is a low-fucose, fully human IgG1-based bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and MET. From a CMC perspective, the case package provided is a clinical multi-discipline review summary and does not contain the full OPQ (Office of Pharmaceutical Quality) technical review dossier. The available record references a Product Quality Review (April 23, 2021), a Quality Executive Summary (April 28, 2021), and a Quality Executive Summary Addendum (May 20, 2021), as well as Drug Substance and Drug Product Microbiology/Facility Reviews, all of which were completed prior to the May 20, 2021 review completion date. The cross-discipline summary indicates no blocking CMC deficiencies were identified by the OPQ reviewer (Andrea Franco) and that facility inspections, comparability strategy, shelf-life, and cell bank qualification were addressed through pre-submission meetings. A post-marketing commitment (PMC) was agreed upon for the tissue-based companion diagnostic IVD, which is a device/CDx matter rather than a drug CMC issue. The low-fucosylation engineering (relevant to ADCC potency and lot-to-lot consistency) and the bispecific format (relevant to aggregation, fragmentation, and charge variant control) are inherent complexity factors for this molecule, but the available record does not surface any unresolved deficiencies in these areas. The formulation (350 mg/7 mL, 50 mg/mL single-dose vial) is straightforward for a monoclonal antibody-class biologic. On the basis of the available record, CMC does not independently block approval, though the complexity of the molecule warrants ongoing post-market stability and comparability vigilance.
key_concerns: Limited CMC detail visible in this case package: the full OPQ technical review (impurity characterization, control strategy, process validation data, extended stability data) is not reproduced here, creating residual uncertainty in this assessment.

Bispecific IgG1 format with low-fucosylation engineering introduces complexity: aggregation, fragmentation, charge variant profiles, and DAR-analog consistency (arm-pairing fidelity) must be tightly controlled and are not directly assessable from the clinical summary alone.

Stability data adequacy (ICH Q1): the pre-submission meetings confirmed a shelf-life strategy and a 30-day post-submission stability update was agreed upon, but the actual stability data package and confirmed shelf-life claim are not visible in this review document.

Comparability across manufacturing scale-up (Phase I/II material used in CHRYSALIS vs. proposed commercial process): pre-submission meetings addressed this, but the adequacy of the comparability exercise (PK bridging, functional assays, physicochemical characterization) cannot be independently verified from the clinical summary.

Cell bank qualification: a Type B CMC meeting confirmed the qualification strategy for future working cell banks, but the completion status of this qualification at the time of BLA submission is not confirmed in the available record.

Facility inspection status: the Quality Executive Summary and Addendum are referenced but not reproduced; no inspection classification (VAI/NAI/OAI) for the drug substance or drug product manufacturing facilities is explicitly stated in the clinical summary.

Post-marketing commitment for tissue-based companion diagnostic IVD (EGFR exon 20 insertion detection): while primarily a CDRH/CDx matter, the absence of a validated tissue-based test at approval has indirect implications for patient selection quality in the post-market setting.

deficiencies.description: Incomplete CMC data visibility in the case package: The full OPQ technical review covering impurity characterization and control strategy (ICH Q3/Q6B), extended real-time stability data supporting the proposed shelf-life claim (ICH Q1), and process validation data for the commercial-scale bispecific manufacturing process are not reproduced in the available multi-discipline review summary. For a low-fucose bispecific IgG1, these are critical quality attributes. However, the referenced OPQ reviews (April–May 2021) appear to have been completed, and pre-submission meetings resolved key strategic questions. This is assessed as a documentation/visibility gap in the case package rather than a confirmed unresolved deficiency, and is therefore treated as non-blocking pending confirmation that the OPQ review reached an approvable conclusion.

Comparability of CHRYSALIS clinical material to proposed commercial process: Amivantamab used in the pivotal CHRYSALIS study must be demonstrated comparable to the commercial-scale drug product via a robust physicochemical, functional (ADCC, receptor binding, bispecific arm-pairing), and PK bridging package. Pre-submission meetings indicate FDA accepted the comparability strategy, but the adequacy of the executed comparability data cannot be independently confirmed from the clinical summary. If the OPQ review identified residual gaps, this could be approval-limiting. Assessed as non-blocking given the pre-submission alignment, but flagged for confirmation.

Shelf-life and cold-chain stability for a bispecific antibody: The 350 mg/7 mL single-dose vial formulation must have adequate real-time and accelerated stability data (ICH Q1A(R2)) demonstrating control of aggregation, fragmentation, and potency loss over the proposed shelf-life. A 30-day post-submission stability update was agreed upon pre-BLA. The completion and adequacy of this update is not confirmed in the available record. Assessed as non-blocking given the agreed update mechanism, but requires OPQ confirmation.

major_deficiencies.description: Single-arm, non-randomized, open-label pivotal dataset (N=81, CHRYSALIS) with no active comparator arm: causal inference is limited, direct benefit-risk comparison against current second-line standards of care (ramucirumab+docetaxel, single-agent chemotherapy, anti-PD-(L)1 agents) is not possible, and the accelerated approval surrogate endpoint (ORR/DOR) has not yet been verified by a randomized trial demonstrating improvement in OS or PFS. The confirmatory Phase 3 trial (PAPILLON) is ongoing but unreported, leaving the clinical benefit unverified under 21 CFR 601.41.

Companion diagnostic ecosystem gap at launch: only a plasma-based CDx (Guardant360 CDx) was reviewed contemporaneously. Validation of a tissue-based IVD for EGFR exon 20 insertion detection is deferred as a post-marketing commitment, creating a clinically significant diagnostic access gap given that tissue-based NGS remains the predominant testing modality in U.S. oncology practice. Patients who cannot be identified by the approved CDx may be inappropriately excluded from or included in treatment.

Dose optimization deficiency under Project Optimus principles: the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) was selected in a Phase 1 dose-escalation context without a dedicated dose-optimization or dose-ranging study. Formal exposure-response analyses are supportive but not sufficient to establish that the submitted dose represents the optimal benefit-risk balance across the target population, particularly given the high rate of infusion-related reactions (~65%) and rash/paronychia driving dose modifications.
